theme: Lament and prayer; new creation, the grand finale
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 63:15-66:24. The book ends with a desperate prayer for God to tear open the heavens, an answer that announces a new heavens and a new earth, and a final scene of worship and warning. Read chapter 65 slowly. It is the great finale of the book.
settingTheScene: The last part of Isaiah opens with one of the most heartfelt prayers in the Old Testament. The people confess their sin, plead for God to act, and ask for the heavens to be torn open. God replies with a promise of new creation, a place where the LORD’s people live in peace and joy, with long life and no tears. The book closes with a contrast between those who tremble at God’s word and those who do not.
observation: “For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name” (63:16).
“Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence” (64:1).
“We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment” (64:6).
“But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand” (64:8).
“Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear” (65:24).
“For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind” (65:17).
“No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days” (65:20).
“But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (66:2).
interpretation:
The prayer of 63:15 to 64:12 is the plea of a people who feel far from God. They look back to the exodus and ask where God’s zeal has gone. “You, O LORD, are our Father.” Their earthly fathers may not know them, but God does. They confess that they have strayed: “Why, O LORD, do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart?” And the prayer climbs toward a cry: “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down!” They want God to appear as he did at Sinai.

Then comes the confession of 64:6: “We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.” It is a startling statement. Even our best deeds, apart from God, are stained. No one calls on his name or rouses himself to take hold of God. And then the prayer rests on a relationship: “But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter.” If God shapes us, we can trust the shaping.

God’s answer in chapter 65 begins with a rebuke, because he was ready to be sought by a people who did not ask. “I said, Here am I, here am I, to a nation that was not called by my name.” Yet he will preserve a remnant, his servants, who will inherit. And the grand promise: “I create new heavens and a new earth.” The vision includes Jerusalem as a joy, with no weeping, no early deaths, no frustrated labor. “They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit.” The wolf and the lamb feed together again.

Chapter 66 emphasizes humility. The temple cannot contain God, and he looks to the one who is humble and contrite and trembles at his word. The book ends with a vision of all nations coming to worship, and a sober picture of the fate of rebels. “All flesh shall come to worship before me.” The last note is a warning, so that the reader will choose well.
connection: Mark 1:10 describes the heavens being torn open at Jesus’ baptism, an answer to Isaiah 64:1. Romans 10:20-21 quotes Isaiah 65:1-2 about God’s welcome to the Gentiles. 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1-4 describe the new heavens and new earth, with God dwelling with his people and wiping away every tear. Romans 9:21 draws on the potter and the clay. Philippians 3:9 says our righteousness comes from God by faith. Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24 in Mark 9:48.
application:
Pray Isaiah 64:8 as your own: “You are the potter; I am the clay.” Ask him to keep shaping you.

Consider where you still depend on your “righteous deeds.” Rest in Christ’s righteousness.

Meditate on the new creation. Ask God to make you long for it.
prayerPrompts: Call on God as Father and Redeemer.
Confess that your righteous deeds are like a polluted garment, and tell him whom you trust.
Thank him for the new heavens and new earth.
